work_packages.name: An agent writes a game's entities and rules in plain Rust against one crate, and proves them in an ordinary test with no window
work_packages.quality_bar: Game code that reads as plainly as Bevy's `breakout` example with less ceremony: a scene's rule list reads as a description of play, and no line names engine plumbing. Compiler and startup messages as useful as Rust's own, each naming the object, the cause and the next step. Correctness held as `SIM-2D` holds it: one trace, one digest. The reference for how game code reads is the design's worked examples, which the owner approved.

items.statement: In a game with no window and no camera, built from `thrum` alone and stepped through `Game::test()`: (1) a scene's rules run once a tick in the order the scene lists them, and a rule reads what earlier rules of the same tick wrote to components and resources; (2) an entity spawned in a tick is first visited in the next tick; an entity despawned in a tick is still visited by later rules of that tick and by none after it, and a second `despawn` of it in that tick returns false; a component put on or taken off a living entity with `Attach` is seen from the next tick; (3) a query visits entities in the same order on every run, and its `With` and `Without` filters select as written; (4) a component is known to the world, with no list written by the game, when the signature of a rule, a condition or an enter function names it, and a component that is only ever spawned is known once its scene says `scene.component::<T>()`; a template function spawns what it returns; (5) an event sent by a rule is read by later rules of that tick and by none in the next; (6) a rule or group under `when` runs only in ticks where its condition holds; (7) `par_each` leaves the world as the serial loop does; (8) the first scene given to `Game` is where a game starts, and `go_to` changes scene when the tick ends, after which the entities of the scene left are gone and its resources remain. Guard: CPU tests on worlds of a few entities, in `./dev check`.

A scripted run of a test game that spawns, despawns, writes components and resources and draws from `Random`: (1) gives one world digest at every tick when run twice, when rewound to a tick inside the run and replayed, and when the same game is built again from its scene functions; (2) has a digest that covers the whole world: changing one field of one component, changing one field of one resource, spawning one entity and despawning one entity each give another digest; (3) `Random` gives the same draws for the same seed, tick and request, and other draws for another seed; (4) a rule that returns an error refuses its tick, in a tick where earlier rules had already written a component, written a resource, spawned an entity and despawned one: afterwards every component value, resource value and entity count read back through the harness is what it was before the tick, the error names the rule and the tick, and the next `step()` runs as if the refused tick had not been tried; (5) on the Mac, a rule that panics is reported the same way, with the same values read back. Guard: CPU tests on small worlds, in `./dev check`.

Each of these mistakes is refused with a message that names the object, the cause and the next step, and leaves the world unchanged where a world exists. At compile time: a component or a resource with a `Vec`, a `String`, a reference or a raw float field. At startup, from `test()`, before any tick: two parameters of one rule that write the same component; a rule that reads a resource no scene provides. While running: a spawn of a component that no signature names and no scene declares, whose message names the rule, the component and `scene.component`; `go_to` a scene the game was not given; a spawn past the world's size; a rule that returns an error. A game whose scenes have no camera, no binding and no frame function starts and steps with no complaint. The tests hold each message's object, cause and next step by its text. Guard: in `./dev check`.

No public item of `thrum` names a type of `wgpu`, `winit` or another engine crate by that crate's path. Every public item of `thrum` has a doc comment with an example, and every example runs as a doc test. A package that names `thrum` with default features off builds alone and has no renderer, window, GPU, network or platform crate in its dependency closure. `thrum` and any crate it is built from are registered in `.config/architecture.toml`. Guard: the surface check and the doc tests run in `./dev check` from this landing, so every later work package's additions are held to them.
items.check: python3 scripts/sdk_surface.py check && cargo test --locked --offline -p thrum --doc

items.statement: The SDK is a layer over the engine's simulation and adds no second one.
items.ask: Read `thrum`'s rules half and the tests' games. 1. Is world state held anywhere but `thrum-core`'s registered simulation: is there a second store, clock or undo? 2. Is the loop over entities inside a rule monomorphised for that rule's parameters, with no dynamic call and no allocation for each entity, and no allocation for each tick once warm? One call for each rule each tick through the engine's registered callback is as designed. 3. Does a component's schema identity come from its name and fields, and never from a Rust type ID? 4. Are the changes made in `thrum-core` additions only, with its existing tests unedited and passing? 5. Does any test's game name a crate other than `thrum`, or a schema number, permit, executor, page or device?

items.statement: Game code for the headless subset is written as the design's worked examples write it. Every difference between the built API and the parts of the examples that the design's section "What WP1 compiles" lists is a line in the module's log, and none is a change of shape as the design defines one: a concept added that a game maker must learn, one of the twelve words removed, a change to what a rule sees or to when spawns land, plumbing moved into game code, or a game made to name an engine crate.
items.ask: Set the tests' games beside the parts of the worked examples that the design's section "What WP1 compiles" lists: from example A, `Score`, `drop_rocks`, `fall` and two scenes joined by `go_to`; from example D, `Run`, `Phase`, `enemies_die`, `start_wave`, `end_wave`, the two conditions and the grouped rule list under `when`. Set the rule parameters beside these rows of mechanism 3's table: `Query`, `Res` and `ResMut`, `Entities`, `Attach`, `Events` and `Emit`, `Tick`, `Random` and `Scenes`. Leave out what that section gives to later work packages: looks, cameras, input, commands, players, `per_player`, `Space2d`, number literals and `run()`. List each difference in how a game maker writes the same thing. Is each one in the log as a spelling? Is any a change of shape? A change of shape that is not the owner's own fails this item.

work_packages.name: A crowd of 10,000 written on the SDK, steered by four players, steps identically on the Mac, in Chrome and on the iPhone simulator, and costs what the hand-written crowd does
work_packages.quality_bar: Determinism as Factorio holds it: the same inputs give the same world on every machine, checked by digest. Speed as the engine's own reference crowd: the layer is not what a tick is spent on. Rules that read as example D of the design does.

items.statement: Input reaches rules in three forms and no other, in a game stepped through `Game::test()`. Actions: an action a scene declares with `scene.action` or `scene.bind` is read through `inputs.of(player)` as `held`, `pressed`, `axis` and `stick` at the tick a scripted player's input is admitted, with `pressed` true for one tick. Commands: a command the harness sends for a player is read by `Commands<T>` at one tick, once, after that player's earlier commands, with who sent it; sending when the queue of commands on their way is full reports that the command was not taken, and a command not taken is never read. Players: `PlayerJoined`, `PlayerLeft`, `PlayerAway` and `PlayerBack` are read as events at the tick of each, and a game stepped with no roster script has one player who joins at the first tick. A scene is given `PlayerJoined` at its first tick for every player already in the game, in slot order: with two players joined in a first scene that spawns nothing, `go_to` a second scene whose rule spawns a character for each `PlayerJoined` leaves two characters, a third player who joins later makes three, and no player ever has two. Per-player rules: a `per_player` function is run once a tick for each player's character with that character's named components, that player's input and the tick; with two players steering different ways each character moves by its own player's input, and the function runs in every tick of its scene whatever conditions hold for the rules around it. Guard: CPU tests on small worlds, in `./dev check`.

`Space2d` over entities with a `Collider2d`: `touching`, `within`, `nearest` and `sweep` return what `thrum-sim2d`'s queries return for the same circles, boxes and capsules on the layer asked, less any entity named by `except`, in that index's fixed order. `.on(LAYER)` answers from that layer's colliders alone: `nearest` on one layer returns that layer's nearest collider when colliders of another layer stand nearer, with a radius and without one, and a tie in distance goes to the lower slot. A query with no `.on` returns every layer's answer merged in the same order. Queries answer from where colliders stood when the tick began, and a scene's cell size is part of its rule set. Guard: CPU tests on small worlds, in `./dev check`.

The profile's additions for the SDK are exactly rounded, refuse what a rule may not reach, and change nothing that was retained. Constructing a number from a literal, `Angle` and its direction, turning a `Vec2` and a `Vec3`, and `Quat` products have conformance vectors beside the profile's own. The profile check passes with `thrum`'s rules half as a dependency a rule crate may have, and refuses a rule crate that names `thrum` with its play half. The profile's controls refuse, each with a message that names the reason, a rule crate that reads a file through `std::fs`, opens a socket through `std::net`, starts a process through `std::process` or reads standard input, beside every refusal the profile already made. The reference crowd's retained digests are unchanged. Guard: the vectors, the profile check and its controls run in `./dev check`.
items.check: cargo test --locked --offline -p thrum --test it numbers:: && python3 scripts/sim2d_profile.py check && python3 scripts/sim2d_profile.py controls && cargo test --locked --offline -p crowd-2d --test retained_slice

items.statement: Each of these mistakes is refused with a message that names the object, the cause and the next step. At compile time: reading a `Button` as a stick or an axis, and the like for each kind of action; `per_player` given a function that takes a query, a resource, `Space2d`, `Entities` or `Random`. At startup, from `test()`: a game whose declared actions do not fit an input frame, with the counts and the limit; a command type whose encoding is larger than one action of an input frame may be, with the size and the limit; a `per_player` rule under `when`. While running, each refusing its tick with the world unchanged: a rule that reads an action no scene declares, whose message names the rule, the action and `scene.action` or `scene.bind`; two entities that match one `per_player` rule for one player. The tests hold each message's object, cause and next step by its text. Guard: in `./dev check`.

On the Mac, `crowd-sdk` gives the digests its retained trace holds, and its trace row carries these witnesses, each more than nothing: for each of the four players, how far their hero moved along the direction that player's script steers, the four scripts steering up, down, left and right; hits; deaths; respawns; the angle the turning body turned through; and ticks a rule refused by returning an error at a scripted tick, after each of which the components and resources read back were what they were before it. `crowd-sdk` is a rule crate that names only `thrum`: four players' heroes moved by their input through a `per_player` rule, enemies that chase the nearest hero and keep apart with `par_each`, shots at the nearest enemy that sweep, hits, deaths and respawns, and a body that turns by an `Angle` each tick, at 10,000 bodies. Record: the Mac arm of the three-target conformance run. A slice of the trace, with its witnesses, stays as a CPU test in `./dev check`.
items.check: python3 scripts/sim2d_conformance.py run --package crowd-sdk --target mac-metal && cargo test --locked --offline -p crowd-sdk --test it retained::

items.statement: In Chrome, `crowd-sdk` gives the digests its retained trace holds, with every witness WP2.5 names more than nothing. The conformance runner takes Chrome's lock itself around its browser run, so the item names none. Record: the Chrome arm of the three-target conformance run.

On the iPhone simulator, `crowd-sdk` gives the digests its retained trace holds, with every witness WP2.5 names more than nothing. Function only. The conformance runner takes the simulator for each of its turns itself, so the item names no lock. Record: the simulator arm of the three-target conformance run.

On the Mac, two release takes each of `crowd-sdk` and of the reference crowd at 10,000 bodies report the cost of a tick, of a rewind and of a replay, and the allocations of a warmed tick, side by side, with the build and the load on the machine. The takes of `crowd-sdk` are of the load WP2.5 describes: the record carries, counted over the measured ticks, each of the four players' hero movement, hits, deaths and respawns, each more than nothing, beside the reference's own witnesses for its takes. The record flags for investigation a `crowd-sdk` tick more than about 25% above the reference's, and any allocation in a warmed `crowd-sdk` tick. The check fails only on a missing measurement or a missing witness. The record also names the default number of entities a world holds and why. Record: SDK rule cost beside the hand-written reference, taken under load.
`crowd-sdk` reads as example D of the design does, and what the SDK added to the engine for it belongs to the engine's owners.
items.ask: 1. Read `crowd-sdk`'s rules beside example D. Does each rule read as one thing the game does? Does the package hold a helper file that hides plumbing a game maker would have to write: registration, encoding, scheduling, index building? Count every file of the package as game lines. 2. Is each difference from the design's examples in the log as a spelling, and is none a change of shape? 3. Are the profile's additions in `thrum-core`'s profile, with no platform maths call, and do the reference crowd's rules and retained traces stand unedited? 4. Does `Space2d` build one `thrum-sim2d` index for each layer once a tick, keep its storage between ticks, and answer a query on a layer from that layer's index alone, so that an enemy's nearest-hero query looks at the heroes and not at the crowd? 5. Is the heroes' `per_player` function their whole movement step, writing the pose itself, with nothing in it but its character's components, its player's input and the tick?

items.statement: A game outside the engine checkout that keeps its rules in a rule crate of its own, laid out as the design's `multiplayer` template is (a game package with a path to its own rule crate, each reaching the engine by path), passes the engine's external game check and the profile check of its own rule crate. The same game with raw-float arithmetic in its rules, and again with a file read in its rules, fails its own profile check with a message that names the violation, while the engine's check of its registered rule packages still passes. The external game check still refuses a game package that names an engine example and a path that leaves the game's folder for anything but the engine's crates. Guard: a test over a scratch game outside the checkout, in `./dev check`.
